task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-06-19, in the area of play-type labeling and data quality):
Opponent next-possession PPP after you run play X is large enough to drive AVOID labels; own-sequence lags similarly matter.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

methodological_questions: sample size and power for specific play types

historical_evidence.finding: Play-type actions have decaying cross-possession memory (lag-1 effect >= lag-2; not just score margin or team quality). Observed result: FAIL decay-sanity: DRIVE lifts +0.015,+0.020,+0.018,+0.021,+0.020 (flat). Within-team: DRIVE lag-1 +0.015 to -0.002. Cohen d ~0.01-0.03; p~0 from n>150k. Callable play-type horizons = 0. Verdict: failed_gate.

Higher AVOID share predicts losing, independent of team quality. Observed result: Game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 (inflated n, team-quality confound). Series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered; ~80 series needed for p<0.05). Low AVOID-share bin 52.6% vs 25-50% bin 37.0%. Verdict: inconclusive.

A specific opponent play type on the preceding possession suppresses each star's next-possession PPP relative to that star's baseline. Observed result: PUTBACK is top suppressor for 6+ stars (e.g. D. Mitchell 1.178 to 0.884, d=-0.294, n_after=95; B. Beal d=-0.345 n=32; C. Holmgren d=-0.222 n=52). Other tops: TRANSITION (A. Davis -0.058), POST_UP (N. Jokic -0.075), PULL_ [cut; read_family for the full text].

Specific opposing lineups, defenders, play types and preceding opponent play types suppress star efficiency. Observed result: Q5c verdict 'rank-1 suppressor varies meaningfully across players'; e.g. Jokic after opp POST_UP 1.1271 (-0.0675, SE +/-0.0500, n=480); Curry forced POST_UP -0.209. Verdict: inconclusive.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempt to establish decaying cross-possession memory of play-type actions on subsequent outcomes.
failed_approaches.why: C_artifact (apparent effect produced by a construction, selection or labelling flaw); flat non-decaying lifts collapsed under within-team baseline; team-quality confound.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Attempt to show higher AVOID share predicts losing independent of team quality at the series level.
failed_approaches.why: A_unanswerable (question not answerable with the data or design); series n=50 p=0.07; still confounded by team quality; underpowered (needed ~80 series).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Identifying specific opponent play types that suppress a star's next-possession PPP.
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from [prior work]); no multiplicity correction; n_after (sample size for specific play types) was small (32-95) compared to thousands for baseline possessions.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Identifying specific factors (lineups, defenders, play types) that suppress star efficiency, including sequential triggering.
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear (mechanism unclear from [prior work]); rank-1 deltas mostly within 1-2 SE with no multiple-comparison control; OTHER artifact flagged.

evidence_establishes: Lagged effects of play types on subsequent possessions are measurable but highly susceptible to confounding by team quality and potential artifacts from data construction or selection ([prior work][prior work]).
Team quality is a critical confounder that must be controlled for when analyzing play-type impacts or AVOID labels ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).

The concept of 'AVOID' labels exists within the project context, and its relationship to winning has been explored but found untestable/inconclusive due to confounding and sample size issues ([prior work][prior work]).

Analyzing specific play-type interactions or player-specific sequential effects often leads to small sample sizes for individual cells, necessitating careful consideration of statistical power and multiplicity correction ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether 'AVOID' labels are directly driven by opponent next-possession PPP or own-sequence lags, as the definition and mechanism of 'AVOID' labels in relation to these outcomes are not detailed.
A robust methodology for cleanly isolating causal lagged effects of play types, free from confounding by team quality or other factors.
The specific magnitude or decay characteristics of cross-possession memory for play types in a way that is not an artifact.
Whether the available data contains sufficient instances of specific play type sequences combined with AVOID labels to achieve adequate power for a detailed analysis.
own_inferences: The research question implies that 'AVOID' labels are a consequence or reflection of poor outcomes, specifically high opponent PPP after a given play or poor own-sequence performance. The definition of 'AVOID' labels is crucial for this analysis.
Controlling for team quality will likely involve using a within-team or matched-game design to mitigate the observed confounding issues.

The 'own-sequence lags' aspect of the question suggests looking at the impact of a play type on subsequent plays run by the same team, not just the opponent, which is a broader scope than some historical work.
uncertainties: The precise definition and generation mechanism of 'AVOID' labels are not detailed in the provided context or historical evidence. This is critical for understanding what drives them.
How to effectively de-confound team quality from play-type effects, especially when looking at cross-possession or lagged impacts.
The frequency of specific play types leading to 'AVOID' labels, which will dictate available sample size for analysis.
The exact meaning of 'large enough to drive AVOID labels' – what threshold or statistical significance is implied?

historical_effect.explanation: The historical evidence significantly changed the decision from a potential 'proceed' to 'proceed_with_changes'. It highlighted critical, previously failed approaches related to confounding (team quality), artifacts in lagged effect measurement, and insufficient power for granular analyses (specific play types, series-level AVOID analysis). Without this evidence, these risks might have been underestimated, leading to a design that would likely reproduce past failures. The evidence compels a more robust design focusing on within-team comparisons, explicit confounder control, and careful consideration of 'AVOID' label definition and sample size.

blocking_constraints.text: Team quality is a significant confounder for both play-type effectiveness and AVOID labels, as shown in previous studies ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]). Failing to control for this will lead to spurious correlations.

The definition and generation of 'AVOID' labels are critical but not explicitly provided. If these labels are poorly defined or inconsistently applied, the entire analysis will be compromised. This also applies to the derived play-type possession records.

Analyzing specific play types and their lagged effects, especially in conjunction with 'AVOID' labels, may lead to small sample sizes for certain combinations, resulting in underpowered analyses ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).

prior_work.summary: Previous work has explored lagged effects of play types on subsequent possessions, but found results to be artifacts due to confounding by team quality ([prior work][prior work]). The relationship between 'AVOID' share and winning was untestable/inconclusive due to confounding and small sample sizes ([prior work][prior work]). Studies on superstar sequential suppression also highlighted issues with small sample sizes for specific play-type interactions and lack of multiplicity control ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]). While these studies touch on components of the current question (lagged effects, PPP, AVOID labels, confounding), none directly answer how opponent next-possession PPP or own-sequence lags *drive* AVOID labels, nor do they provide a robust, artifact-free methodology for this specific causal link.

risks.text: Team quality, score margin, game context (e.g., time of game, opponent strength) can confound the relationship between play types, subsequent PPP, and AVOID labels. A superior team might run 'bad' plays and still have good subsequent PPP, or good teams might generate more 'AVOID' labels for their opponents due to their overall defensive scheme rather than specific play-type triggers.
The reliability and consistency of 'AVOID' labels and derived play-type possession records are critical. Any inconsistency or bias in their generation could invalidate findings.

If 'AVOID' labels are rare, or if specific play type X occurs infrequently, the sample size for particular combinations of (play X, AVOID label, lagged PPP) could be too small to detect meaningful effects with statistical power.
Testing the effects across many different play types or lag sequences without proper multiplicity correction could lead to spurious findings ([prior work][prior work], [prior work][prior work]).

As seen in [prior work][prior work], apparent effects can be artifacts of data construction, selection, or labeling flaws. Careful design is needed to avoid such issues, especially when defining possessions and lags.

design.estimand: The causal effect of running play type X (or an 'own-sequence' lagged effect) on the opponent's next-possession Points Per Possession (PPP), specifically quantifying if this effect is 'large enough' to correlate with or trigger 'AVOID' labels. The 'largeness' will be defined by statistical significance and effect size (e.g., Cohen's d or PPP differential).
design.unit: Basketball possession, defined from the derived play-type possession records. The primary unit of observation will be a 'sequence' (play type X followed by opponent possession) or 'own-sequence' (play type X followed by own team's next possession).
design.sample: All NBA regular season and playoff possessions from 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 (complete portions). We will filter for possessions where play type X is clearly identified and AVOID labels (once defined) are applicable. We will use a within-team design, comparing instances of play type X to a control group of other play types run by the *same team* in similar game contexts, to control for team quality and general game state.
design.power: A priori power analysis will be conducted based on anticipated effect sizes (e.g., minimum detectable PPP difference of 0.05) and observed frequencies of play type X and AVOID labels. The current sample size of multiple NBA seasons should provide sufficient data for overall trends, but specific play-type X / AVOID label combinations may require larger samples. If specific combinations are too sparse (e.g., <500 instances), they will be excluded from detailed analysis.
design.controls: Primary controls: 1. Within-team comparison: analyze effects relative to the average PPP for the same team in similar situations. 2. Game context: Control for score margin, quarter, time remaining, home/away, and opponent quality (e.g., using opponent's season-average PPP allowed). 3. Player presence: Control for key players on court for both teams. 4. Lagged score/possession outcomes: Ensure effects are not merely due to previous possession outcomes (e.g., a turnover leading to high opp PPP).
design.falsification: 1. Test for decay: If a true causal effect, we expect a decaying impact over increasing lags (e.g., lag-1 effect > lag-2). Flat or increasing 'lifts' would suggest an artifact ([prior work][prior work]). 2. Placebo test: Analyze the impact of a 'neutral' or randomly selected preceding event on subsequent PPP and AVOID labels, expecting no significant effect. 3. Reverse causation: Test if AVOID labels predict *preceding* play types (expect no effect if AVOID labels are a consequence).
design.multiplicity: Apply Bonferroni correction or False Discovery Rate (FDR) control for multiple comparisons, especially if analyzing the impact of many different play types X or multiple lag durations. Focus on a pre-defined subset of high-frequency or theoretically relevant play types.
design.decision_rule: The research question will be considered 'supported' if a statistically significant (p < 0.05 after multiplicity correction) and practically meaningful (e.g., Cohen's d > 0.1 or PPP difference > 0.05) effect of play type X on opponent next-possession PPP is consistently observed across teams, and this effect is strongly correlated with the presence of 'AVOID' labels for play type X, after controlling for confounding factors. The 'own-sequence lags' will be assessed similarly. The 'large enough to drive' aspect requires a clear statistical link (e.g., high odds ratio or logistic regression coefficient) between the PPP outcome and the AVOID label. If effects are inconsistent, small, or collapse under controls, the question will be 'rejected'. If data sparsity or uncontrolled confounding prevents robust conclusions, it will be 'untestable'.
design.data_version: Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) from NBA 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 (complete portions) regular season and playoffs. NBA stats API play-by-play data for contextual variables.
